Synset.Definition: The medical assistance program authorized to enable each State to furnish medical assistance on behalf of families with dependent children and of aged, blind, or disabled individuals whose income and resources are insufficient to meet the costs of necessary medical services, and rehabilitation and other services to help such families and individuals attain or retain capability for independence or self-care

The insurance program that provides basic protection against the costs of hospital, related post-hospital, home health services, and hospice care for individuals age 65 or over eligible for Social Security or railroad retirement benefits, individuals under age 65 entitled for not less than 24 months to disability benefits under Social Security or the railroad retirement system, and individuals medically determined to have end stage renal disease

Original Medicare is the Medicare fee-for-service program under parts A and B, through which a Medicare+Choice (Medicare Advantage) eligible individual — an individual entitled to benefits under Part A and enrolled under Part B — may elect to receive Medicare benefits, as the alternative to enrolling in a Medicare+Choice (Medicare Advantage) plan

Medicare Advantage (Part C) is the alternative to Original Medicare through which a Medicare+Choice eligible individual may elect to receive Medicare benefits (other than qualified prescription drug benefits) by enrolling in a Medicare+Choice plan, of which there are three types: coordinated care plans, which provide health care services including health maintenance organization plans and regional or local preferred provider organization plans; Medicare+Choice medical savings account (MSA) plans, paired with a contribution into a Medicare+Choice MSA; and Medicare+Choice private fee-for-service plans

Medicare Part D is the voluntary prescription drug benefit program under which each Part D eligible individual is entitled to obtain qualified prescription drug coverage by enrolling in a prescription drug plan or an MA-PD plan

The Medicare Part D late enrollment penalty increases a Part D eligible individual's premium, for each uncovered month after the individual's initial enrollment period during which the individual went without creditable prescription drug coverage, by 1 percent of the base beneficiary premium computed for that year

Extra Help is the Medicare Part D income-related subsidy program that reduces or eliminates Part D premiums, deductibles, and cost-sharing for individuals with limited income and resources; for the lowest-income group it provides an income-related premium subsidy equal to 100 percent of the relevant premium amount, subject to a specified cap

A Medicare supplemental policy (Medigap policy) is a health insurance policy or other health benefit plan that a private entity offers to a Medicare beneficiary and that is primarily designed, or is advertised, marketed, or otherwise purported, to provide payment for expenses incurred for services and items that are not reimbursed under the Medicare program because of deductibles, coinsurance, or other limitations under Medicare; such policies must meet or exceed the NAIC Model Standards, which is how their benefits are standardized nationally into lettered plans

A dual eligible special needs plan (D-SNP) is a specialized Medicare Advantage plan for special needs individuals who are entitled to medical assistance under a State Medicaid plan, that coordinates the delivery of Medicare and Medicaid services for individuals eligible for such services; may provide coverage of Medicaid services, including long-term services and supports and behavioral health services, for individuals eligible for such services; and has a contract with the State Medicaid agency meeting minimum coordination-of-care requirements

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 435.1101 (implementing 42 USC 1396r-1a, presumptive eligibility for children)
Synset.Definition: Under Medicaid, a period of presumptive eligibility for children begins on the date on which a qualified entity determines that a child is presumptively eligible, and ends with the earlier of the day on which a decision is made on a Medicaid application filed on the child's behalf, or, if no such application has been filed, the last day of the month following the month in which the determination of presumptive eligibility was made

Synset.dc:source: 26 USC 7702B(b)(1) (Title 26 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: A qualified long-term care insurance contract is any insurance contract under which the only insurance protection provided is coverage of qualified long-term care services; that does not pay or reimburse expenses incurred for services or items to the extent reimbursable under Medicare (title XVIII of the Social Security Act), or that would be so reimbursable but for a deductible or coinsurance amount; that is guaranteed renewable; that does not provide for a cash surrender value or other money that can be paid, assigned, or pledged as collateral for a loan, or borrowed; and under which all refunds of premiums and all policyholder dividends or similar amounts are applied as a reduction in future premiums or to increase future benefits

For purposes of the federal requirements for long term care facilities, 'facility' means a skilled nursing facility (SNF) that meets the requirements of sections 1819(a), (b), (c), and (d) of the Social Security Act, or a nursing facility (NF) that meets the requirements of sections 1919(a), (b), (c), and (d) of the Social Security Act

Synset.dc:source: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia (National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health), Do-Not-Resuscitate Order
Synset.Definition: A do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order is a medical order written by a health care provider that instructs providers not to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if a patient's breathing stops or if the patient's heart stops beating

Synset.dc:source: 26 USC 21(b)(1) (Title 26 is not a loaded USC title); IRS Publication 503, Child and Dependent Care Expenses ("Qualifying Person")
Synset.Definition: For the child and dependent care credit, a qualifying individual (called a "qualifying person" in IRS guidance) is: a dependent of the taxpayer who has not attained age 13; a dependent of the taxpayer who is physically or mentally incapable of caring for himself or herself and who has the same principal place of abode as the taxpayer for more than one-half of the taxable year; or the spouse of the taxpayer, if the spouse is physically or mentally incapable of caring for himself or herself and has the same principal place of abode as the taxpayer for more than one-half of the taxable year

Synset.dc:source: 26 USC 21(b)(2)(A) (Title 26 is not a loaded USC title); IRS Publication 503, Child and Dependent Care Expenses ("Work-Related Expenses")
Synset.Definition: Employment-related expenses (called "work-related expenses" in IRS guidance) are amounts paid for household services, and for the care of a qualifying individual, but only if incurred to enable the taxpayer to be gainfully employed for a period during which there is one or more qualifying individuals with respect to the taxpayer; IRS guidance further specifies that an expense is work related only if it allows the taxpayer (or the taxpayer's spouse, if filing jointly) to work or look for work, and is for a qualifying person's care — an expense is not work related merely because it was incurred while the taxpayer was working
Planned or emergency care provided to a child or adult with a special need in order to provide temporary relief to the family caregiver of that child or adult
A coordinated system of accessible, community-based respite care services for family caregivers of children or adults with special needs

Services designed to assist individuals in acquiring, retaining, and improving the self-help, socialization, and adaptive skills necessary to reside successfully in home and community based settings; includes (with exceptions) prevocational, educational, and supported employment services, but does not include special education and related services available to the individual through a local educational agency or vocational rehabilitation services available through a program funded under section 730 of title 29

Services which will assist individuals eligible under the State Medicaid plan in gaining access to needed medical, social, educational, and other services, including assessment of an eligible individual to determine service needs, development of a specific care plan, referral and related activities to help an individual obtain needed services, and monitoring and followup activities to ensure the care plan is effectively implemented and adequately addresses the needs of the individual

The waiver authority under which the Secretary may provide that a State Medicaid plan include as medical assistance payment for part or all of the cost of home or community-based services (other than room and board), approved by the Secretary, which are provided pursuant to a written plan of care to individuals with respect to whom there has been a determination that but for the provision of such services the individuals would require the level of care provided in a hospital or a nursing facility or intermediate care facility for the mentally retarded (the statute's own facility term; current regulations say intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities) the cost of which could be reimbursed under the State plan

Under Medicare, the following items and services furnished to an individual, who is under the care of a physician, a nurse practitioner or a clinical nurse specialist, or a physician assistant, by a home health agency or by others under arrangements with them made by such agency, under a plan established and periodically reviewed by such a practitioner, provided on a visiting basis in a place of residence used as the individual's home: part-time or intermittent nursing care; physical or occupational therapy or speech-language pathology services; medical social services; part-time or intermittent services of a home health aide; medical supplies and durable medical equipment; and certain medical services of a hospital intern or resident-in-training

Under Medicare, an individual is considered confined to his home (homebound) if the individual has a condition, due to an illness or injury, that restricts the ability of the individual to leave his or her home except with the assistance of another individual or the aid of a supportive device (such as crutches, a cane, a wheelchair, or a walker), or has a condition such that leaving his or her home is medically contraindicated; the individual need not be bedridden, but there should exist a normal inability to leave home, leaving home should require a considerable and taxing effort, and absences to receive health care treatment (including adult day-care programs), infrequent or short absences, and absences to attend religious services do not disqualify the individual

A public agency or private organization (or a subdivision thereof) which is primarily engaged in providing hospice care and services, makes such services available (as needed) on a 24-hour basis, also provides bereavement counseling for the immediate family of terminally ill individuals, and provides for such care and services in individuals' homes, on an outpatient basis, and on a short-term inpatient basis

The following items and services provided to a terminally ill individual by, or by others under arrangements made by, a hospice program under a written plan established and periodically reviewed by the individual's attending physician and by the medical director of the program: nursing care; physical or occupational therapy or speech-language pathology services; medical social services; services of a home health aide and homemaker services; medical supplies and the use of medical appliances; physicians' services; short-term inpatient care, including both respite care (only on an intermittent, nonroutine, and occasional basis, not consecutively over longer than five days) and procedures necessary for pain control and acute and chronic symptom management; counseling (including dietary counseling) with respect to care of the terminally ill individual and adjustment to his death; and any other item or service which is specified in the plan and for which payment may otherwise be made under Medicare
An individual is considered to be terminally ill if the individual has a medical prognosis that the individual's life expectancy is 6 months or less

An institution (or a distinct part of an institution) which is primarily engaged in providing to residents skilled nursing care and related services for residents who require medical or nursing care, or rehabilitation services for the rehabilitation of injured, disabled, or sick persons, is not primarily for the care and treatment of mental diseases, and has in effect a transfer agreement with one or more participating hospitals

An institution (or a distinct part of an institution) which is primarily engaged in providing to residents skilled nursing care and related services for residents who require medical or nursing care, rehabilitation services for the rehabilitation of injured, disabled, or sick persons, or, on a regular basis, health-related care and services to individuals who because of their mental or physical condition require care and services (above the level of room and board) which can be made available to them only through institutional facilities, and is not primarily for the care and treatment of mental diseases

Any service, care, or item (including an assistive device), including a disease prevention and health promotion service, an in-home service, and a case management service, intended to assist individuals in coping with, and to the extent practicable compensate for, a functional impairment in carrying out activities of daily living, furnished at home, in a community care setting, or in a long-term care facility, and not furnished to prevent, diagnose, treat, or cure a medical disease or condition

The period before a Medicaid application within which a disposal of assets for less than fair market value makes an individual ineligible for certain long-term care benefits: the look-back date is 36 months (or, in the case of payments from certain trusts or of any other disposal of assets made on or after February 8, 2006, 60 months) before the first date on which an institutionalized individual both is institutionalized and has applied for medical assistance, or before the date a noninstitutionalized individual applies for medical assistance or, if later, disposes of assets for less than fair market value

The requirement that a State seek adjustment or recovery of medical assistance correctly paid on behalf of an individual under the State Medicaid plan: from the individual's estate or upon sale of property subject to a Medicaid lien, and, in the case of an individual who was 55 years of age or older when the individual received medical assistance, from the individual's estate for medical assistance consisting of nursing facility services, home and community-based services, and related hospital and prescription drug services (or, at the option of the State, any items or services under the State plan)

A program of all-inclusive care for the elderly that is operated by a PACE provider, provides comprehensive health care services to PACE program eligible individuals in accordance with the PACE program agreement and regulations, and provides assistance in obtaining necessary transitional care when an individual's enrollment ceases
An area agency on aging designated under section 3025(a)(2)(A) of title 42 or a State agency performing the functions of an area agency on aging under section 3025(b)(5)

An entity, network, or consortium established by a State as part of the State system of long-term care to provide a coordinated and integrated system for older individuals and individuals with disabilities, and their caregivers, that provides comprehensive information on available public and private long-term care programs, options, service providers, and resources; person-centered counseling to assist individuals in assessing their existing or anticipated long-term care needs and developing and implementing a person-centered plan; access to the full range of publicly-supported long-term care services and supports; and information and referrals regarding available home and community-based services for individuals who are at risk for residing in, or who reside in, institutional settings

The Older Americans Act Title III-E program under which the Assistant Secretary for Aging makes grants to States with approved State plans, to pay the Federal share of State programs enabling area agencies on aging (or entities they contract with) to provide multifaceted systems of support services for family caregivers and for older relative caregivers, which may be informed through the use of caregiver assessments

Under the Older Americans Act, an adult family member, or another individual, who is an informal provider of in-home and community care to an older individual or to an individual of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder with neurological and organic brain dysfunction; under the Lifespan Respite Care Act, an unpaid family member, a foster parent, or another unpaid individual, who provides in-home monitoring, management, supervision, or treatment of a child or adult with a special need

A caregiver who is age 55 or older and lives with, is the informal provider of in-home and community care to, and is the primary caregiver for, a child or an individual with a disability; in the case of a child, the grandparent, stepgrandparent, or other relative (other than the parent) by blood, marriage, or adoption who is the primary caregiver because the biological or adoptive parents are unable or unwilling to serve and who has a legal relationship to the child or is raising the child informally; in the case of an individual with a disability, the parent, grandparent, or other relative by blood, marriage, or adoption

Under the Older Americans Act (for purposes of the exploitation definitions), an individual who has the responsibility for the care of an older individual, either voluntarily, by contract, by receipt of payment for care, or as a result of the operation of law, and means a family member or other individual who provides (on behalf of such individual or of a public or private agency, organization, or institution) compensated or uncompensated care to an older individual

A defined process of gathering information to identify the specific needs, barriers to carrying out caregiving responsibilities, and existing supports of a family caregiver or older relative caregiver, as identified by the caregiver involved, to appropriately target recommendations for support services; administered through direct contact with the caregiver, which may include contact through a home visit, the Internet, telephone or teleconference, or in-person interaction
An individual who is 60 years of age or older

A community facility for the organization and provision of a broad spectrum of services, which shall include provision of health (including mental and behavioral health), social, nutritional, and educational services and the provision of facilities for recreational activities for older individuals

A severe, chronic disability of an individual that is attributable to a mental or physical impairment or combination of mental and physical impairments; is manifested before the individual attains age 22; is likely to continue indefinitely; results in substantial functional limitations in 3 or more of the following areas of major life activity: self-care, receptive and expressive language, learning, mobility, self-direction, capacity for independent living, and economic self-sufficiency; and reflects the individual's need for a combination and sequence of special, interdisciplinary, or generic services, individualized supports, or other forms of assistance that are of lifelong or extended duration and are individually planned and coordinated

Services, supports, and other assistance, provided to families with members who have developmental disabilities, that are designed to strengthen the family's role as primary caregiver, prevent inappropriate out-of-the-home placement of the members and maintain family unity, and reunite families with members who have been placed out of the home whenever possible

Activities that result in individuals with developmental disabilities, with appropriate assistance, having the ability and opportunity to communicate and make personal decisions; the ability and opportunity to communicate choices and exercise control over the type and intensity of services, supports, and other assistance the individuals receive; the authority to control resources to obtain needed services, supports, and other assistance; opportunities to participate in, and contribute to, their communities; and support, including financial support, to advocate for themselves and others
The statutory umbrella term of the National Alzheimer's Project Act: in that Act, the term Alzheimer's means Alzheimer's disease and related dementias

Services, not otherwise furnished under the State's Medicaid plan, that are furnished under a waiver granted under 42 CFR part 441, subpart G. They may include case management services, homemaker services, home health aide services, personal care services, adult day health services, habilitation services, respite care services, day treatment or other partial hospitalization services, psychosocial rehabilitation services and clinic services for individuals with chronic mental illness, and other services requested by the State agency and approved by CMS as cost effective and necessary to avoid institutionalization

Synset.dc:source: CMS 1915(c) Waiver Technical Guide v3.6 (Jan. 2019), Appendix C (Homemaker) (elaborated definition)
Synset.Definition: Services that consist of the performance of general household tasks (for example, meal preparation and routine household care) provided by a qualified homemaker, when the individual regularly responsible for these activities is temporarily absent or unable to manage the home and care for him or herself or others in the home; listed as one of the services a State may cover under a Medicaid HCBS waiver at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(2)

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 409.45(b); listed as a waiver service at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(3)
Synset.Definition: Visits by a home health aide to provide hands-on personal care, or services needed to maintain the person's health or facilitate treatment of an illness or injury — for example bathing, dressing, grooming, hair, nail and oral hygiene, feeding, assistance with elimination, assistance with ambulation, changing position in bed, and assistance with transfers

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 440.167; listed as a waiver service at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(4)
Synset.Definition: Services furnished to an individual who is not an inpatient or resident of a hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities, or institution for mental disease, that are authorized for the individual by a physician in accordance with a plan of treatment or, at the option of the State, otherwise authorized in accordance with a service plan approved by the State; provided by an individual who is qualified to provide the services and who is not a member of the individual's family; and furnished in a home, and at the State's option, in another location

Synset.dc:source: CMS 1915(c) Waiver Technical Guide v3.6 (Jan. 2019), Appendix C (Adult Day Health) (elaborated definition)
Synset.Definition: Services generally furnished 4 or more hours per day on a regularly scheduled basis, for one or more days per week, or as specified in the service plan, in a non-institutional, community-based setting, encompassing both health and social services needed to ensure the optimal functioning of the participant; listed as one of the services a State may cover under a Medicaid HCBS waiver at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(5)

Medicare coverage of home health services for a beneficiary who is confined to the home (homebound); is under the care of a physician or allowed practitioner; needs intermittent skilled nursing care, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, or continuing occupational therapy; and is under a plan of care, with services furnished by or under arrangement with a Medicare-participating home health agency

An individualized written plan that specifies the care and services necessary to meet the patient-specific needs identified in the comprehensive assessment, identifies the responsible discipline(s) and patient-specific measurable outcomes and goals, and is established, periodically reviewed, and signed by a doctor or allowed practitioner
Patient and family-centered care that optimizes quality of life by anticipating, preventing, and treating suffering

Services and supports provided to beneficiaries of all ages who have functional limitations and/or chronic illnesses that have the primary purpose of supporting the ability of the beneficiary to live or work in the setting of their choice, which may include the individual's home, a worksite, a provider-owned or controlled residential setting, a nursing facility, or other institutional setting

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 441.505; statutory six-activity list (eating, toileting, transferring, bathing, dressing, continence) at 26 USC 7702B(c)(2)(B)
Synset.Definition: Basic personal everyday activities including, but not limited to, tasks such as eating, toileting, grooming, dressing, bathing, and transferring

Activities related to living independently in the community, including but not limited to, meal planning and preparation, managing finances, shopping for food, clothing, and other essential items, performing essential household chores, communicating by phone or other media, and traveling around and participating in the community

Synset.dc:source: 26 USC 7702B(c)(2)(A) (Title 26 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: An individual certified by a licensed health care practitioner within the preceding 12 months as: unable to perform, without substantial assistance from another individual, at least 2 activities of daily living for a period of at least 90 days due to a loss of functional capacity; having a similar level of disability; or requiring substantial supervision to protect the individual from threats to health and safety due to severe cognitive impairment

The initial evaluation of an individual's need for the level of care provided in a hospital, a nursing facility, or an intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (required when there is a reasonable indication that the individual might need such services in the near future), together with periodic reevaluations, at least annually, of each beneficiary receiving home or community-based services to confirm the continued need for that level of care

The process for developing an individual's person-centered service plan, which must be led by the individual (and the individual's authorized representative, if applicable); include people chosen by the individual; provide necessary information and support to ensure the individual directs the process to the maximum extent possible; occur at times and locations convenient to the individual; reflect cultural considerations and use plain language; include strategies for solving conflict or disagreement; offer informed choices regarding services and supports; and exclude providers of HCBS for the individual from developing the plan, except under the limited conflict-of-interest exception where no other willing and qualified entity is available

The written plan produced by the person-centered planning process, which must reflect the services and supports that address the individual's identified functional needs and preferences, including the setting in which the individual resides as chosen by the individual; the individual's strengths and preferences; clinical and support needs identified through an assessment of functional need; individually identified goals and desired outcomes; the services and supports (paid and unpaid) and the providers of them, including natural supports; and risk factors and measures in place to minimize them; written in plain language and finalized with the individual's informed written consent

Refers to families, children, aged, blind, or disabled individuals, and pregnant women who are not categorically needy but who may be eligible for Medicaid because their income and resources are within limits set by the State under its Medicaid plan, including persons whose income and resources fall within these limits after their incurred expenses for medical or remedial care are deducted

The process by which a person whose income or resources exceed the State's medically needy Medicaid limits becomes eligible by deducting incurred expenses for medical or remedial care, so that income and resources fall within the medically needy limits

Synset.dc:source: Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, Pub. L. 109-171, sec. 6071; Medicaid.gov, Money Follows the Person
Synset.Definition: A Medicaid demonstration program that supports state strategies to rebalance long-term services and supports from institutional to community-based care, awarding grants to states to transition Medicaid participants who reside in institutional settings, such as nursing facilities, into community-based settings, and to eliminate barriers that restrict use of Medicaid funds so eligible individuals can receive LTSS in the setting of their choice

Supportive services provided in the home under the Older Americans Act, including homemaker, personal care, home care, home health, and other aides; visiting and telephone or virtual reassurance; chore maintenance; respite care for families, including adult day care; and minor home modification necessary to facilitate the independence and health of older individuals

The opportunity for participants or their representatives to exercise choice and control over the budget, planning, and purchase of self-directed personal assistance services, including the amount, duration, scope, provider, and location of service provision, with participant decision-making authority that includes recruiting, hiring and discharging, scheduling, and supervising workers; under the Community First Choice rule, a consumer controlled method of selecting and providing services and supports that allows the individual maximum control, with the individual acting as the employer of record or having a significant and meaningful role in the management of an agency provider

Under the Medicaid Access Rule, any of the following individuals who deliver home and community-based services (employed or contracted by a Medicaid provider, State agency, or third party, or working under a self-directed model): a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist providing nursing services; a licensed or certified nursing assistant; a direct support professional; a personal care attendant; a home health aide; or other individuals paid to provide services addressing activities of daily living or instrumental activities of daily living, behavioral supports, employment supports, or other services to promote community integration

Synset.dc:source: President's Committee for People with Intellectual Disabilities, Report to the President 2017 (elaborated definition)
Synset.Definition: A direct care worker who provides services and supports that empower people with intellectual and developmental disabilities to live, work, and participate in the community, such as assistance with daily living, employment supports, and community integration; listed as a direct-care-worker category at 42 CFR 441.302(k)(1)(ii)(C)

A direct care worker paid to provide personal care services — hands-on assistance with activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living — to a person in their home or community; listed by name, without further elaboration, as a direct-care-worker category in the governing regulation

Significantly subaverage general intellectual functioning, existing concurrently with deficits in adaptive behavior and manifested during the developmental period, that adversely affects a child's educational performance (the federal IDEA definition; formerly termed 'mental retardation' before Rosa's Law)

An alternative to guardianship where individuals retain their right to make decisions for themselves, with the support of trusted individuals they choose; trusted supporters can be family, friends, neighbors, faith community members, affinity groups, and personal services

A legal process in which a state court finds a person incapacitated pursuant to state law and appoints someone else to make decisions on behalf of that person; guardianships may be limited in scope, state laws generally allow guardianship only as a last resort, and courts must consider less restrictive alternatives such as supported decision-making

The most common form of dementia — a brain disorder that slowly destroys a person's memory and thinking skills, characterized by a loss of cognitive functioning (thinking, remembering, and reasoning) and behavioral abilities to such an extent that it interferes with a person's daily life and activities; caused by changes in the brain including abnormal buildups of proteins known as amyloid plaques and tau tangles, with symptoms typically first appearing in the mid-60s

Synset.dc:source: NIA, What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis
Synset.Definition: The loss of cognitive functioning — thinking, remembering, and reasoning — and behavioral abilities to such an extent that it interferes with a person's daily life and activities; a general term covering a range of conditions, of which Alzheimer's disease is the most common form

Synset.dc:source: NIA, What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis
Synset.Definition: A form of dementia caused by conditions that damage blood vessels in the brain or interrupt the flow of blood and oxygen to the brain

Synset.dc:source: NIA, What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis
Synset.Definition: A form of dementia caused by abnormal deposits of the protein alpha-synuclein, called Lewy bodies

Synset.dc:source: NIA, What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis
Synset.Definition: A rare form of dementia that tends to occur in people younger than 60; it is associated with abnormal amounts or forms of the proteins tau and TDP-43
A combination of two or more types of dementia — for example, some people have both Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia

Synset.dc:source: NIA, What Is Mild Cognitive Impairment?
Synset.Definition: A condition in which some older adults have more memory or thinking problems than other adults their age; risk increases with age, and conditions such as diabetes, depression, and stroke may increase a person's risk. It is not dementia, but people with MCI are at greater risk of developing dementia

Synset.dc:source: NIA, Coping With Agitation, Aggression, and Sundowning in Alzheimer's Disease
Synset.Definition: When restlessness, agitation, irritability, and confusion happen or worsen as daylight begins to fade — in the late afternoon or early evening — in a person with Alzheimer's disease or another dementia; being overly tired can increase late-afternoon and early-evening restlessness

In dementia care, walking away from home or from a caregiver, common among people with Alzheimer's disease, with the risk of becoming lost; caregivers are advised to limit wandering and prevent the person from becoming lost through identification, locks, and community awareness

Synset.dc:source: CMS State Operations Manual, Appendix PP, F-tag 689 (interpretive guidance under the general "Accidents" condition of participation, 42 CFR 483.25(d), which does not itself use the term "elopement")
Synset.Definition: In long-term care, when a resident leaves the premises or a safe area without authorization (i.e., an order for discharge or leave of absence) and/or any necessary supervision to do so — the facility-care counterpart of wandering, treated as a serious safety event in nursing facility oversight

Specialized dementia care provided in special Alzheimer's care units — often separate sections of a nursing home or assisted living facility — where staff members have special training to care for people with dementia, providing special activities, meals, medical care, and environments designed to feel more like home

A residential facility with rooms or apartments for people who may need some help with daily tasks but do not need around-the-clock care; some assisted living facilities have special Alzheimer's units with staff who check on and care for people with dementia, and residents pay for the room or apartment and may pay extra for special care

A home for people who can no longer care for themselves, in which several people receiving care live together with at least one caregiver on site at all times; staff make meals, help with grooming and medication, and provide for other needs

Synset.dc:source: 34 CFR 104.33(b); 29 USC 794 (Title 29 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: A 504 plan is an educational plan under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 through which a public school provides a qualified student with a disability the regular or special education and related aids and services designed to meet that student's individual educational needs as adequately as the needs of students without disabilities are met

Synset.dc:source: 20 USC 1401(9) (Title 20 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Free appropriate public education (FAPE) is special education and related services that have been provided at public expense, under public supervision and direction, and without charge; meet the standards of the State educational agency; include an appropriate preschool, elementary school, or secondary school education in the State involved; and are provided in conformity with the individualized education program required under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act

Synset.dc:source: 20 USC 1412(a)(5)(A) (Title 20 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Least restrictive environment (LRE) is the IDEA requirement that, to the maximum extent appropriate, children with disabilities are educated with children who are not disabled, and that special classes, separate schooling, or other removal from the regular educational environment occurs only when the nature or severity of the disability is such that education in regular classes with the use of supplementary aids and services cannot be achieved satisfactorily

Synset.dc:source: 20 USC 1401(1)(A); 34 CFR 300.5 (Title 20 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Assistive technology (an assistive technology device) is any item, piece of equipment, or product system — whether acquired commercially off the shelf, modified, or customized — that is used to increase, maintain, or improve the functional capabilities of a child with a disability

Synset.dc:source: 38 USC 1720G(b); 38 CFR 71.40 (Title 38 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: The Program of General Caregiver Support Services (PGCSS) is the VA program of support services for caregivers of covered veterans who are enrolled in the VA health care system, including caregivers who do not reside with the veteran, offering services such as counseling, training, and referral

Client responsibility (also called patient liability, resident liability, client share, recipient liability, or share of cost) is the portion of an institutionalized or waiver Medicaid recipient's own income that they must apply toward the cost of their care each month — their total income minus a personal needs allowance and other permitted deductions such as a spousal or family allowance and incurred medical expenses — with Medicaid paying the remainder

Consultation services in self-directed care are the support system of information, counseling, training, and assistance that helps a participant (or the participant's family or representative) identify, access, manage, direct, and purchase the personal assistance services and supports in their service plan and budget

The Consumer Directed Employer (CDE) is, in Washington State, a private entity that contracts with the state to serve as the legal employer of individual home-care providers, handling employment functions such as payroll while the client continues to select and direct their own provider

The proper use of benefits, for a Social Security representative payee, is using the benefits they receive for the beneficiary's current maintenance — the beneficiary's food, shelter, clothing, medical care, and personal comfort needs — which is how SSA judges that benefits have been properly used

For the IRS child and dependent care credit, an individual is physically or mentally not able to care for oneself (incapable of self-care) if, because of a physical or mental defect, they are incapable of caring for their own hygiene or nutritional needs, or require the full-time attention of another person for their own safety or the safety of others
A ward of the state is a person placed under the protection, care, or guardianship of another — such as the state — because they are a minor or have been found legally incapacitated

Synset.dc:source: American Council on Aging, Medicaid Planning Assistance, What is the Medicaid marriage penalty?
Synset.Definition: The Medicaid marriage penalty is the loss of Medicaid eligibility that can result when marriage combines a couple's income and assets so that their counted totals exceed the program's needs-based limits

Synset.dc:source: 29 USC 705(17) (Title 29 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Independent living core services are, under the Rehabilitation Act, the required services of a Center for Independent Living: information and referral services; independent living skills training; peer counseling, including cross-disability peer counseling; individual and systems advocacy; and services facilitating transition from institutions to the community, diversion from institutionalization, and youth transition to postsecondary life

Synset.dc:source: 5 USC 8903c (Title 5 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Postal Service Health Benefits (the PSHB Program) is a program within the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, administered by the Office of Personnel Management, under which carriers offer health plans to eligible Postal Service employees and annuitants and their families

The Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) is the notice a Medicare Advantage or Part D plan must send its enrollees each fall — at least 15 days before the annual coordinated election period — describing the plan's cost and coverage changes taking effect the following January 1 (also called the Annual Notice of Coverage)

Star Ratings are CMS's one-to-five-star ratings of the quality and performance of Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, built from individual measure-level star ratings that are combined into summary and overall ratings to help beneficiaries compare plans

Supplemental benefits are services a Medicare Advantage plan may offer in addition to those covered by Original Medicare — provided either as mandatory benefits included for all enrollees or as optional benefits an enrollee may elect and pay for — subject to CMS approval

Synset.dc:source: CMS/NAIC, Choosing a Medigap Policy (2025); 42 USC 1395ss
Synset.Definition: Medigap Plan C is a standardized Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan that covers Part A and Part B coinsurance, the Part A and Part B deductibles, skilled nursing facility coinsurance, and foreign-travel emergency care; because it pays the Part B deductible, Plan C is closed to people first eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020

Synset.dc:source: CMS/NAIC, Choosing a Medigap Policy (2025); 42 USC 1395ss
Synset.Definition: Medigap Plan N is a standardized Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan that pays 100 percent of the Part B coinsurance except for copayments of up to 20 dollars for some office visits and up to 50 dollars for emergency-room visits that do not lead to inpatient admission, and that does not cover the Part B deductible or Part B excess charges

A facility fee is a separate charge, paid under Medicare's Outpatient Prospective Payment System, for a hospital outpatient department's use of its rooms, equipment, supplies, and support resources when an outpatient service is furnished there, billed in addition to the practitioner's professional fee

Synset.dc:source: National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys (NAELA), What Is Elder Law?
Synset.Definition: Elder law is a holistic area of legal practice that integrates the legal system with the social and medical concerns of older adults and people with disabilities, encompassing planning, counseling, education, and advocacy on matters such as long-term care, guardianship, estate and special-needs planning, and public benefits

Synset.dc:source: Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin, Fast Fact: Caregiver Burden (concept originating with Zarit, Todd and Zarit, The Gerontologist, 1986)
Synset.Definition: Caregiver burden is the extent to which providing care has an adverse effect on the caregiver's emotional, social, financial, physical, and spiritual functioning

Synset.dc:source: NINDS (National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke), Parkinson's Disease
Synset.Definition: Early-onset Parkinson's disease (also called young-onset Parkinson's disease) is Parkinson's disease that begins before age 50, which occurs in a small percentage of people with Parkinson's disease

An individualized education program (IEP) is a written statement for each child with a disability that is developed, reviewed, and revised in a meeting by an IEP team in accordance with the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, setting out the child's present levels of academic achievement and functional performance, measurable annual goals, and the special education and related services to be provided

Synset.dc:source: 34 CFR 303.20; 20 USC 1436 (Title 20 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: An individualized family service plan (IFSP) is a written plan for providing early intervention services under Part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act to an infant or toddler with a disability and that child's family, based on evaluation and assessment and implemented with parental consent

Synset.dc:source: 20 USC 1431 et seq.; 34 CFR part 303 (Title 20 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act is the federal program of early intervention services for infants and toddlers with disabilities (from birth through age two) and their families, delivered through an individualized family service plan

Transition planning is, under IDEA, the coordinated set of transition services planned in a child's IEP within a results-oriented process focused on improving the child's academic and functional achievement to facilitate movement from school to post-school activities such as postsecondary education, vocational training, integrated employment, independent living, and community participation

Synset.dc:source: Center on PBIS (OSEP-funded), What is PBIS?; the framework is referenced in IDEA at 20 USC 1414(d)(3)(B)(i)
Synset.Definition: Positive behavioral interventions and supports (PBIS) is an evidence-based, tiered framework for supporting students' behavioral, academic, social, emotional, and mental health; implemented with fidelity it improves social-emotional competence, academic achievement, and school climate

Synset.dc:source: 38 CFR 3.352(a); 38 USC 1521(d) (Title 38 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: Aid and attendance is a U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs determination — and the increased pension it provides — that a claimant, because of disability, needs the regular aid and attendance of another person for everyday functions such as dressing, keeping ordinarily clean and presentable, feeding, or protection from the hazards and dangers of daily living

Synset.dc:source: 38 CFR 71.15; 38 CFR 71.35 (Title 38 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: A general caregiver, in the VA caregiver program, is a person who is not a designated Primary or Secondary Family Caregiver and who provides personal care services to a covered veteran, whether or not the person resides with the veteran

Synset.dc:source: MACPAC, Report to Congress on Medicaid and CHIP, ch. 5 (June 2025); Section 1115 of the Social Security Act
Synset.Definition: Cash and Counseling was a Section 1115 Medicaid demonstration (in Arkansas, Florida, and New Jersey) that let beneficiaries eligible for personal assistance and home-and-community-based services choose a cash allowance plus counseling and fiscal support to self-direct their own services in lieu of agency-directed services

Synset.dc:source: Applied Self-Direction, The Fiscal/Employer Agent: An Overview; 26 USC 3504; IRS Rev. Proc. 2013-39
Synset.Definition: A Fiscal/Employer Agent (F/EA) is, in Medicaid self-direction, an IRS Section 3504 agent that, on behalf of self-directing home-care employers, processes payroll and withholds, deposits, and reports employment taxes following IRS Revenue Procedure 2013-39

Synset.dc:source: MACPAC, Report to Congress on Medicaid and CHIP, ch. 5 (June 2025)
Synset.Definition: Financial management services (FMS) are administrative supports in Medicaid self-direction that handle the fiscal tasks of being an employer; the primary models are the Fiscal/Employer Agent (split into Government F/EA and Vendor F/EA), under which the beneficiary is the common-law employer, and Agency with Choice, under which the agency is the common-law employer and the beneficiary is the co-employer or managing employer

Institutional deeming is a Medicaid rule that lets a state cover a home- and community-based-services waiver participant living in the community by treating them as if they were institutionalized, so that only the participant's own income and resources are counted for eligibility rather than a spouse's or parents' income being deemed available

Synset.dc:source: American Council on Aging, Medicaid Planning Assistance, Income Protection and Medicaid Waivers
Synset.Definition: The protected income level (PIL) is the amount of a Medicaid home- and community-based-services recipient's monthly income that the state lets them keep for ordinary living expenses such as rent, utilities, and food, with income above that level applied toward the cost of care; the exact amount is set by each state

For Medicaid and SSI purposes, legally disabled means unable to engage in any substantial gainful activity by reason of a medically determinable physical or mental impairment that can be expected to result in death or that has lasted or can be expected to last for a continuous period of not less than 12 months

Fair market value, in the Medicaid transfer-of-assets (look-back) context, is an estimate of the value an asset would have sold for at the prevailing market price at the time it was actually transferred, against which any uncompensated transfer is measured

Imminent risk of institutional placement is, as defined by Florida's Medicaid Long-Term Care waiver rule, the situation of a person living at home or in the community who is unable to perform self-care because of a deteriorating physical or mental health condition, has no capable caregiver, and is likely to be placed in a nursing facility within about one to three months

Synset.dc:source: CMS Informational Bulletin, Coverage of Housing-Related Activities and Services for Individuals with Disabilities (June 26, 2015)
Synset.Definition: Housing and tenancy-based case management comprises Medicaid-coverable housing supports for people with disabilities, older adults, and those experiencing chronic homelessness: pre-tenancy housing transition services (assessment, housing search and application, and move-in support) and ongoing tenancy sustaining services that help a person maintain a lease and avoid eviction once housed

The Medicaid annual review is the requirement that most beneficiaries' eligibility be renewed (redetermined) once every 12 months, and no more frequently than once every 12 months, to confirm they still qualify

Synset.dc:source: California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS), Medi-Cal
Synset.Definition: Medi-Cal is California's Medicaid program, which provides free or low-cost health coverage to eligible low-income California residents

Synset.dc:source: Ohio Department of Medicaid, MyCare Ohio
Synset.Definition: MyCare Ohio is Ohio's managed-care demonstration that coordinates care under a single plan for Ohioans who are dually eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid

Synset.dc:source: Maryland Department of Health, ACIS Program
Synset.Definition: The ACIS Program is Maryland's Assistance in Community Integration Services program, a Medicaid program that provides housing-related case management and supports to enrollees who are experiencing or at risk of homelessness

Synset.dc:source: Indiana Family and Social Services Administration, Aged and Disabled Waiver; 42 USC 1396n(c)
Synset.Definition: An Aged and Disabled Waiver is a Medicaid Section 1915(c) home- and community-based services waiver that funds in-home and community supports as an alternative to nursing-facility care for aged individuals and people with disabilities who would otherwise require an institutional level of care

Synset.dc:source: New Jersey Department of Human Services, Personal Preference Program (PPP)
Synset.Definition: The Personal Preference Program (PPP) is New Jersey's Medicaid self-direction option that lets NJ FamilyCare/Medicaid members who qualify for Personal Care Assistant services direct those services themselves, including selecting and managing their own workers, to remain independent at home and in the community

Synset.dc:source: New Mexico Administrative Code 8.314.6 (Mi Via waiver)
Synset.Definition: In-home living supports are, under New Mexico's Mi Via waiver, individualized services delivered in the recipient's own home that instruct or enhance home-living skills and address health and safety, enabling the recipient to live in their own house or apartment

Synset.dc:source: Georgia Department of Community Health, About Us
Synset.Definition: The Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH) is the Georgia state agency that serves as the lead (single state) agency administering Georgia's Medicaid and PeachCare for Kids programs

Synset.dc:source: Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services (DMAS), Consumer Directed Services
Synset.Definition: The Virginia CDS Program (Consumer-Directed Services) is Virginia Medicaid's service-delivery model in which the member (or the member's designated representative) acts as the employer of their own personal-care attendant — hiring, training, managing, and if necessary terminating the attendant
Public Partnerships LLC (PPL) is a financial management services company that administers payroll and fiscal supports for Medicaid self-directed and consumer-directed care programs across many states

NHS Continuing Healthcare (CHC) is, in England, a package of health and social care that is arranged and funded solely by the NHS for an adult whose need for care is primarily due to a significant ongoing health need (a primary health need)

A Medicare Savings Program is a Medicaid-administered program (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary, Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary, or Qualifying Individual) that pays some or all of a low-income Medicare beneficiary's Part A and Part B premiums and, for the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary group, cost-sharing

Synset.dc:source: CMS Innovation Center, Guiding an Improved Dementia Experience (GUIDE) Model
Synset.Definition: The GUIDE Model is a voluntary CMS Innovation Center payment model (Guiding an Improved Dementia Experience) that funds interdisciplinary dementia-care teams to deliver care coordination and management, caregiver education and support, respite services, and 24-hour support-line access, so that people living with dementia can remain in their homes and communities

The Part D coverage gap was the former phase of Medicare Part D drug coverage, after the initial coverage limit, in which enrollees paid a larger share of their drug costs (the donut hole); the coverage gap applied only to years before 2025 and has been replaced by a capped annual out-of-pocket structure

The Part D coverage phases are the phases a standard Medicare Part D benefit moves through within a plan year — an annual deductible phase, then a coinsurance (initial coverage) phase, and, once the annual out-of-pocket threshold is reached, a catastrophic phase in which the enrollee pays nothing further — which is why a beneficiary's drug costs change over the course of the year

The Medigap open enrollment period is the one-time six-month period beginning with the first month in which a person is both age 65 or older and enrolled in Medicare Part B, during which a Medigap insurer may not deny or condition issuance of a policy, or discriminate in its pricing, because of the applicant's health status, claims experience, receipt of health care, or medical condition

Medigap premium rating is the method by which a Medigap policy's premium is set: community-rated (the same premium regardless of age), issue-age-rated (the premium is based on the age at which the policy is bought and does not rise with age), or attained-age-rated (the premium is based on the policyholder's current age and rises as they get older)

Synset.dc:source: National Research Council, The Role of Human Factors in Home Health Care (2010), Schulz and Tompkins, Informal Caregivers in the United States
Synset.Definition: An informal caregiver is a person — often a family member — who provides typically unpaid care to someone with whom they have a personal relationship

Synset.dc:source: Alzheimer's Association, Treatments for Alzheimer's and Dementia, alz.org/alzheimers-dementia/treatments (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: There is no cure for Alzheimer's disease; treatments exist that may change disease progression, and drug and non-drug options may help treat symptoms, but none reverses or cures the underlying disease

Synset.dc:source: Parkinson's Foundation, What Is Parkinson's Disease?, parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/what-is-parkinsons (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: There is no cure for Parkinson's disease; treatment options include medications, lifestyle adjustments, and surgery to manage symptoms, but none cures the underlying disease

Synset.dc:source: Parkinson's Foundation, What Is Parkinson's Disease?, parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/what-is-parkinsons (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: Parkinson's disease itself is not fatal, but complications from the disease can be serious; the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rated complications from Parkinson's disease as the 14th leading cause of death in the United States

Parkinson's disease is not typically directly inherited: almost 90% of people with Parkinson's have no known genetic variant contributing to their disease, and only around 10% have a form of Parkinson's caused by an inherited genetic variant that affects multiple family members; the disease results from a complex interaction of genetic and environmental factors, and even people who inherit a risk-associated variant are not guaranteed to develop the disease
A movement disorders specialist is a neurologist with specialized training in movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease

Synset.dc:source: Lewy Body Dementia Association, Caregiver FAQ
Synset.Definition: Dementia with Lewy bodies is not typically directly inherited; most cases occur without a known family history, and rare familial forms linked to specific gene variants are the exception rather than the rule

Synset.dc:source: AFTD (Association for Frontotemporal Degeneration), FAQs, theaftd.org/what-is-ftd/faqs/
Synset.Definition: Frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) has a known genetic cause in roughly a third of cases (an inherited gene variant); the remaining, sporadic cases have no identified cause. Traumatic brain injury and environmental or toxin exposure are not established causes of FTD specifically — distinct from the separate, injury-associated neurodegenerative condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy

Synset.dc:source: National Institute on Aging, What Is Dementia?
Synset.Definition: Alzheimer's disease and most other dementias are progressive and irreversible brain disorders; no diet or nutritional change reverses the underlying neurodegeneration, though treating a co-occurring reversible cause of cognitive impairment (for example a vitamin deficiency) is a distinct question from reversing dementia itself

Synset.dc:source: Hospice Foundation of America, Common Questions, hospicefoundation.org/common-questions/
Synset.Definition: Hospice care neither hastens nor postpones death; it is comfort-focused care for a person with a life-limiting illness, aimed at managing pain and symptoms and supporting quality of life, not at accelerating the dying process

Synset.dc:source: Hospice Foundation of America, Common Questions, hospicefoundation.org/common-questions/
Synset.Definition: Grief does not follow a single universal or strictly sequential set of stages; people grieve in individual ways and on individual timelines, and a stage-based model should not be read as prescribing what every griever must feel or when

Synset.dc:source: American Occupational Therapy Association, What Is Occupational Therapy?, aota.org/about/what-is-ot (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: An occupational therapist is a practitioner who helps people of all ages participate in the activities they want and need to do in daily life — activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, and eating; adaptive equipment recommendations; caregiver and family training; falls prevention and home safety; and returning to work, school, or leisure — using everyday activities themselves as the therapeutic intervention

Under England and Wales's Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person lacks mental capacity in relation to a decision if, at the material time, they are unable to make that decision for themselves because of an impairment of, or a disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain; the impairment or disturbance may be permanent or temporary, capacity cannot be assumed merely from a person's age, appearance, or a condition or aspect of behaviour, and the question is decided on the balance of probabilities

For Medicaid trust purposes, if a trust established by the individual (or their spouse) is revocable, the entire corpus of the trust is considered a resource available to the individual, payments from the trust to or for the individual's benefit are considered the individual's income, and any other payment from the trust is considered a disposal of assets by the individual for transfer-penalty purposes

For Medicaid trust purposes, if a trust established by the individual (or their spouse) is irrevocable, any portion of the trust from which payment could under any circumstances be made to or for the individual's benefit is considered a resource available to the individual (or income, if paid), while any portion from which no payment could under any circumstances be made to the individual is treated as a disposal of assets, subject to the transfer-penalty look-back rules, as of the date the trust was established — meaning an irrevocable trust is not automatically safe from Medicaid; unlike a revocable trust, it also generally cannot simply be undone once its non-payable portion has triggered a transfer penalty

A Medicaid applicant may transfer assets to, or to a trust established solely for the benefit of, the applicant's child who is blind or permanently and totally disabled, without incurring a transfer-of-assets penalty period, unlike most other asset transfers made during the look-back period

The "snapshot date" (the statute's own term is the "assessment") is the date — the beginning of the institutionalized spouse's first continuous period of institutionalization — as of which the couple's total combined countable resources are valued to compute the community spouse resource allowance; either spouse may request that the State perform and document this assessment, and it is not a date either spouse chooses on their own

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396r-5(c); 42 USC 1396a(a)(10)(C)(i)(III) (Medicaid's adoption of SSI resource-counting methodology)
Synset.Definition: A countable asset (countable resource) is an asset that Medicaid counts toward an applicant's resource limit for eligibility; Medicaid counts only the applicant's own resources and, where the applicant is married, the couple's combined countable resources under the spousal-impoverishment resource rules — not the resources of other people living in the applicant's household, such as adult children or in-laws, who are not the applicant's spouse

Medicare Part B covers pneumococcal, influenza, COVID-19, and Hepatitis B vaccines and their administration as preventive vaccines, generally with no coinsurance or deductible; other commercially available vaccines (for example, the shingles vaccine) are covered instead under Part D

Medicare Part B covers screening mammography subject to conditions on facility certification and frequency based on the beneficiary's age, at 100 percent of the Medicare payment amount with no coinsurance or deductible

Medicare Part B covers an annual screening for depression as an "additional preventive service" the Secretary added through the national coverage determination process, at no coinsurance or deductible to the beneficiary
Medicare Part B covers ambulance services when transportation in any other vehicle would endanger the beneficiary's health, subject to medical-necessity certification requirements

Medicare Part D excludes coverage of agents used for anorexia, weight loss, or weight gain from its formulary, the same excluded-drug category Medicaid programs may apply under section 1927(d)(2) of the Social Security Act; a GLP-1 medication prescribed specifically for weight loss falls within this exclusion, though the same drug may be covered under Part D when prescribed for a different, non-excluded FDA-approved indication such as diabetes

Medicare Part B covers specified telehealth services delivered by an interactive telecommunications system between an eligible practitioner and a beneficiary, subject to originating-site, geographic, and eligible-service conditions set by statute and expanded temporarily and by waiver in various periods

Medicare does not cover the room-and-board or custodial-care costs of assisted living, because Medicare excludes custodial care from coverage; Medicare may still cover separately-billable, medically-necessary services (such as physician visits, home health, or hospice) delivered to a beneficiary who happens to reside in an assisted living facility

For a Medicare beneficiary who also has employer-sponsored retiree health coverage (as opposed to coverage through current active employment), Medicare generally pays first and the retiree plan pays second, coordinating benefits as a secondary payer under Medicare's coordination-of-benefits framework

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 422.2 (definition underlying the D-SNP eligibility population); 42 CFR 447.20 (Medicaid payer-of-last-resort principle, fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: A dual eligible individual is a Medicare beneficiary who is also entitled to medical assistance under a State Medicaid plan; for services covered by both programs, Medicaid is the payer of last resort, paying only after Medicare and other liable third parties have paid their share

The Fall Open Enrollment Period — CMS's Annual (Coordinated) Election Period — runs from October 15 through December 7 each year; during it, a Medicare beneficiary may switch between Medicare Advantage plans, move between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage, or change Part D drug plans, for coverage effective the following January 1

A Special Enrollment Period lets a Medicare beneficiary change plans outside the standard enrollment windows when a qualifying life event occurs — including moving to a new address outside the current plan's service area

Synset.dc:source: see, e.g., Pennsylvania's filial support statute, 23 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 4603 (representative example)
Synset.Definition: A filial responsibility (filial support) law is a state statute imposing a duty on an adult child to support an indigent parent; roughly two dozen states have such laws, and where they exist they run from child to parent, not between siblings — there is no general legal duty for siblings to financially support one another

A Medicaid- or Medicare-participating nursing facility may not require a third party, including a resident's agent under a power of attorney, to personally guarantee payment from the third party's own funds as a condition of the resident's admission or continued stay; an agent signing admission paperwork in a representative capacity does not thereby become personally liable for the resident's nursing home debt

Federal financial participation is not available for a Medicaid home- and community-based-services waiver expenditure for room and board, except for a limited short-term respite-care circumstance; room and board is therefore not itself a covered HCBS waiver service

Synset.dc:source: Public Partnerships (PPL), New York CDPAP Frequently Asked Questions, pplfirst.com/new-york-cdpap-frequently-asked-questions/ (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: A Client Identification Number (CIN) is a unique identifier New York State assigns to a person once they are approved for Medicaid, used to manage the person's Medicaid benefits and services; it is printed on the person's Medicaid card (an eight-character code) and can also be obtained from the Medicaid helpline or the person's Local Department of Social Services

Community Direct Support/Navigation is a New Mexico Mi Via waiver service that helps a self-directing participant explore activities, hobbies, social events, and educational programs and make connections in the community, with guidance from a community provider or support broker toward the participant's independence
